      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "3.1 Environmental needs",
      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-framework-for-water-resources-2025-water-for-growth-nature-and-a-resilient-future/3-how-much-additional-water-we-need-national-framework-for-water-resources-2025#environmental-needs",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-framework-for-water-resources-2025-water-for-growth-nature-and-a-resilient-future/3-how-much-additional-water-we-need-national-framework-for-water-resources-2025#environmental-needs",
        "text": "\u003cp\u003eThe quantification of changes to current and future abstraction needed to meet environmental requirements is known as the Environmental Destination for water resources.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cdiv role=\"note\" aria-label=\"Information\" class=\"application-notice info-notice\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003eThe \u003cstrong\u003eEnvironmental Destination\u003c/strong\u003e for water resources identifies where, and by how much, water abstraction needs to change to achieve and maintain a healthy water environment, both now and in the future.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Environmental Destination defines the long-term environmental outcomes to ensure abstraction from rivers, groundwater, lakes, wetlands and estuaries is environmentally sustainable, both to address current unsustainable abstraction and future pressures. ​​It identifies where and by how much abstraction may need to reduce to meet current and future environmental requirements for nature. It considers both legal requirements and government commitments. It includes known challenges and assessments of the future potential impact of climate change and considers growth.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe detailed technical approach to assessing environmental needs is contained in Appendix C: Environmental Destination technical report. This includes how we use this includes how we use environmental flow targets to identify where changes to abstraction may be required.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe figures presented here are a high-level indication of need. They have been adjusted downwards to reflect the actions already included in the 2024 round of water company water resources management plans. They are based on national data sets and analysis and do not include where there may be additional local environmental requirements. They have not been adjusted to reflect any ‘overriding public interest’ decisions which may be made in the future. The figures may also need to be refined as the growth agenda is reflected in Regional Water Resources Plans.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThey allow for better evidence to be used to refine the assessments locally and are the starting point for regional water resources groups to take the national figures and to refine them as they develop regional plans. We will provide supplementary technical guidance to advise regional groups on how to include Environmental Destination needs within their plans. Where water companies have sources within or affecting Wales (to supply England), Natural Resources Wales provides guidance on how to meet Welsh legislation Environmental Destination requirements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"figure-5-environmental-requirements-at-a-water-body-level\"\u003eFigure 5: Environmental requirements at a water body level\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThese maps show river waterbodies where abstraction may need to be reduced to meet environment needs at a Q95 low flow. Three maps show the potential abstraction reduction that may be needed now and by the 2050s.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"map-1-current-situation-potential-abstraction-reduction-by-waterbody-in-todays-climate\"\u003eMap 1: Current situation: potential abstraction reduction by waterbody in today’s climate\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/684069b31d85c6606009cd54/s960_Figure-5-Map-1.png\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp\u003eMap 1 shows potential abstraction reductions against today’s baseline environmental requirements. The baseline shows that there is a potential need to reduce fully licensed abstraction by up to 3,200 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e to address current unsustainable abstraction. Of the total estimated abstraction reductions required to meet environmental requirements, approximately 60% is to address current unsustainable abstraction, and of this, water company abstraction accounts for approximately 90% of the reductions needed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"map-2-situation-with-climate-change-and-full-environmental-expectations-potential-abstraction-reduction-by-waterbody-in-2050\"\u003eMap 2: Situation with climate change and full environmental expectations: potential abstraction reduction by waterbody in 2050\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/684069bbe550203c8209cd45/s960_Figure-5-Map-2.png\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp\u003eMap 2 shows how this may change by the 2050s with inclusion of full environmental expectations and with climate change (dry scenario). For this scenario, by the 2050s, this total need could rise to 5,400 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e (full expectations).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"map-3-situation-with-climate-change-full-environmental-expectations-and-after-wrmp24-actions-delivered-potential-abstraction-reduction-by-waterbody-in-2050\"\u003eMap 3: Situation with climate change, full environmental expectations and after \u003cabbr title=\"water resource management plan 24\"\u003eWRMP24\u003c/abbr\u003e actions delivered: potential abstraction reduction by waterbody in 2050\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/684069c2cb73e8b12647b424/s960_Figure-5-Map-3.png\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp\u003eMap 3 shows the remaining potential abstraction reductions following delivery \u003cabbr title=\"water resource management plan 24\"\u003eWRMP24\u003c/abbr\u003e actions (dry scenario). If we take account of plans identified in the 2024 round of water company water resources management plans the environmental requirements could reduce to 2,700 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e (full expectations).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://engageenvironmentagency.uk.engagementhq.com/data-publications-water\"\u003edata behind these maps is available from the Environment Agency’s Water Hub\u003c/a\u003e and is presented at a water body scale.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor an explanation of the development and history of the Environmental Destination figures, please see our technical report. This explains how the figures have evolved and how our understanding of the scale of the challenge has improved.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Environmental Destination will result in a pressure on some, but not all, abstraction licences in those water bodies identified in the analysis. For public water supplies, this is likely to drive a need for additional options to ensure that water remains in the environment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEnvironmental Destination quantifies the potential reductions that could potentially be required to abstraction to meet these environmental requirements. By presenting this analysis, it could be interpreted that there will be a need to require abstraction reductions across all licences in a catchment as the solution. This is not the case. Many abstractions will already be environmentally sustainable because they include conditions to protect flows and levels; for example, some licences will authorise abstraction to fill storage reservoirs at high flows only, avoiding pressures on low flows. The licences most at risk of change will be permanent licences in areas of greatest water stress which do not adequately protect protected site objectives, low flows or groundwater levels.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAddressing unsustainable abstractions will affect supply/demand balances across all sectors of use and will drive the need for additional demand management activity and resource development (in sustainable sources). We set out our approach for action in Section 5.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe will continue to refine our assessment of environmental need. In determining future environmental requirements, we will recognise that as climate change impacts are felt by the environment, natural flows will change, and the environmental needs of the future will reflect this changed environment. We will look at how abstraction licensing should accommodate these changing needs and how protection should be provided for important water dependent nature conservation sites within this evolving landscape, whilst providing a framework for water users to effectively plan water resources for the future.\u003c/p\u003e"
      }
    },

      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-framework-for-water-resources-2025-water-for-growth-nature-and-a-resilient-future/3-how-much-additional-water-we-need-national-framework-for-water-resources-2025#pws-needs",

        "text": "\u003cp\u003eBy 2055, the nation will need up to an additional 5 billion litres of water per day for \u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e under a Do Nothing scenario. This is enough to fill Wembley Stadium almost 4.5 times every day.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe previous National Framework for Water Resources (2020) identified that up to 3,435 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e would be needed from \u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e between 2020 and 2050 without continued action.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis was revised upwards to 4,800 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e by 2050 in 2024 following water company assessments in water resources management plans. The increase was due to updated demand forecasts, additional reductions associated with protecting and improving the environment, and better representation of the baseline supply position without drought measures included.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe modelling for the 2025 National Framework for Water Resources shows that the headline deficit is 4,940 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e by 2055.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cdiv role=\"note\" aria-label=\"Information\" class=\"application-notice info-notice\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003eOur modelling work uses a baseline of 2030 and takes account of the ambitious delivery of actions outlined from 2025 to 2030 in water company water resource management plans. If delivered fully, these actions reduce the deficit to 4,370 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e by 2055. This figure is used in our detailed modelling analysis.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003cp\u003eNationally, as highlighted in Figure 6, \u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e accounts for 87% of current water consumption based on fully licensed abstractions. Of \u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e, water use from households (\u003cabbr title=\"household\"\u003eHH\u003c/abbr\u003e) currently accounts for 58% of water put into supply. This is followed by non-households (\u003cabbr title=\"non-households\"\u003eNHH\u003c/abbr\u003e), such as businesses and industry with use at around 20%. Leakage still makes up a large percentage of current \u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e use, at 19%.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3   \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"row\"\u003ePercentage\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e58\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e100\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003cp\u003eCurrent \u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e availability is already under pressure. Figure 7 highlights that in 2025, there are already water resource zones without a surplus. Nationally, the average availability in 2025 across water resource zones is approximately 7 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e. In some parts of England, water companies are not currently accepting requests for new water for some new non-domestic supplies. This could affect economic growth.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"figure-7-wrmp24-final-plan-supply-demand-balances-in-2025-taken-from-the-latest-available-water-resource-management-plans\"\u003eFigure 7: \u003cabbr title=\"water resource management plan 24\"\u003eWRMP24\u003c/abbr\u003e final plan supply demand balances in 2025 taken from the latest available water resource management plans\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: some water resource zones observe a surplus of only 0 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e, this is an artefact of modelling within water company plans.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/685be2d57d72089d199760f0/s960_Figure-7-NFWR.png\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003ctable\u003e\n  \u003cthead\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eWater resource zone\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eWater company\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\" on supply\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e0\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e453.24\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e505.04\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e452.41\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"row\"\u003eSupply demand balance\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e-4,371.30\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e-1,565.97\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e277.87\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e2,317.76\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003cp\u003eFigure 8 shows the range of national future \u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e needs by 2055 under the modelled scenarios (referred to as supply demand balance). This could range from 0 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e (where we see a surplus of almost 2,320 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e under the Low water needs scenario) to an additional need (deficit) of up to 4,370 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e under the Do Nothing scenario. This is a range of around 6,700 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e. Even with the delivery of all the resource development in company plans and 60% of the demand management reductions currently planned (as presented in the High water needs scenario) there is still a deficit. It shows that delivery of the actions identified through water resources planning (under Central and Low scenarios) can achieve a surplus but strongly highlights the importance of delivering resource development and demand management actions in current plans to resolve those deficits.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe national pressures that contribute to the overall supply-demand-balance vary significantly across each of the modelled scenarios as highlighted in Figure 9.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFuture water needs will vary at a regional, water company and water resource zone scales across the modelled scenarios. This is outlined in Figure 9. Whilst the nation may observe an overall surplus, there are still deficits observed at a water company resource zone scale. The full range of modelled outputs are described in detail at the regional scale in Appendix A.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"figure-9-future-pws-availability-under-the-modelled-scenarios-maps\"\u003eFigure 9: Future \u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e availability under the modelled scenarios (maps)\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eKey:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edarkest red: -700 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edarkest blue: 700 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"low\"\u003eLow\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/681dc70428d7e2f937743a9a/s960_Figure-9-low.png\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"central\"\u003eCentral\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/681dc724c66deec8488f7e4c/s960_Figure-9-central.png\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"high\"\u003eHigh\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/681dc73eced319d02c906041/s960_Figure-9-high.png\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"do-nothing\"\u003eDo Nothing\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/681dc766f16c0654b1906043/s960_Figure-9-do_nothing.png\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp\u003eUnder two of the modelled scenarios, England will observe a water supply deficit in 2055. \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"figure-10-the-drivers-of-the-national-deficit-by-2055-under-the-do-nothing-scenario-mld\"\u003eFigure 10: The drivers of the national deficit by 2055 under the Do Nothing scenario (\u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ctable class=\"js-barchart-table mc-auto-outdent\"\u003e\n  \u003cthead\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eDriver\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003c/th\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/thead\u003e\n  \u003ctbody\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"row\"\u003eDemand from household growth\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e990\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"row\"\u003eResilience move to 0.2% annual chance of drought failure\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e630\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"row\"\u003eClimate change impact to supply\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e340\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"row\"\u003eEnvironmental needs impact on supply\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e2,600\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs shown in Figure 10, under the Do Nothing scenario, the water required to meet the needs of the environment is the biggest driver of future need at a national level, with 2,600 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e forecast to be required by 2055 due to reductions in abstraction to meet current legal environmental requirements and government ambition (taken from \u003cabbr title=\"water resource management plan 24\"\u003eWRMP24\u003c/abbr\u003e). Nationally, demand from household population growth is the second biggest driver of the deficit under Do Nothing with an increase of 990 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e of additional need compared to current baseline. A major component of the last round of \u003cabbr title=\"water resources management plans\"\u003eWRMPs\u003c/abbr\u003e was to ensure that there is increased water supply resilience for people and business where systems are expected to be resilient to a 0.2% annual chance of failure caused by a drought (meaning a 1:500 return period) by 2039. This increased resilience adds an additional 630 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e to the Do Nothing deficit by 2055 under all scenarios at a national scale compared to the baseline. The changing climate puts additional pressure on water availability. Climate change as a driver for future demand is forecast to impact supply by 340 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e. Please note that Figure 10 only shows the main drivers and does not represent all components of the supply demand balance. For more information, please refer to the water resources modelling technical report.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe individual and combined pressures on public water supplies can also be shown at a water company water resource zone scale. Figure 11 shows how climate change, environmental needs, population, drought resilience and in combination pressures drive a need for additional capacity between 2030 and 2055. The figure quantifies this pressure as \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e as a proportion of water supplied (distribution input) in each water company water resources zone, under the Do Nothing scenario.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 11: The total estimated additional capacity required to meet each pressure individually and in combination by 2055 (as a proportion of the water supplied (distribution input)) under a Do Nothing         "text": "\u003cp\u003eOur future estimates of non-public water needs, show that the total additional consumptive water requirements for other sectors by the 2050s could be 1090 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e. This includes an assessment of future water needs for carbon capture and storage and hydrogen production which estimates that 767 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e will be needed by 2050 (see chapter 7).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNationally, spray irrigation has a high projected increase in water consumption with a potential increase of 170 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e. The food and drink, chemicals and paper and pulp sectors show a potential increase of 30, 20 and 5 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e of water consumption respectively by the 2050s.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"baseline-use\"\u003e3.3.1 Baseline use\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt is not just water companies that provide water for business and water using sectors. Water users who abstract directly from the water environment are currently licensed for 114,000 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e and abstract 28,000 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e of freshwater from rivers and groundwater. This demand is forecast to increase to 33,000 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e by the 2050s (not adjusted for consumptiveness).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 proportion of abstraction from freshwater by purpose and adjusted for consumptiveness, excluding navigation. The charts show both excluding and including \u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e . \u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e is the largest water abstractor.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(Abstraction related to navigation has been excluded from this assessment. This is because not all abstractions and transfers to support navigation have been represented in the \u003cabbr title=\"water resources geographical information systems\"\u003eWRGIS\u003c/abbr\u003e abstraction datasets used in this assessment; some navigation transfers may have been accounted for elsewhere as complex activities in the \u003cabbr title=\"water resources geographical information systems\"\u003eWRGIS\u003c/abbr\u003e. For more information on abstracted related to navigation, please refer to the water resources modelling technical report.)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf \u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e use is excluded, under recent actual abstraction rates (and adjusted for consumptiveness), the industry sector uses the most water nationally at 37%, followed by agriculture (30%) and then power (23%). Under fully licensed quantities (adjusted for consumptiveness) the split is very similar to recent actual, with the industry sector at 34%, agriculture at 33% and power generation reduced to 20%.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"figure-13-recent-actual-consumptive-non-public-water-abstraction-by-regional-group-in-mld\"\u003eFigure 13: Recent actual consumptive non-public water abstraction by  \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"row\"\u003eTotal\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e211\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd from freshwater outside the water industry, excluding navigation. The graphs show how this differs across the regional groups. In the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Resources West\"\u003eWRW\u003c/abbr\u003e geography, industry is the biggest non-\u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e water user at 56%, followed by agriculture at 23%. This is a similar pattern in the \u003cabbr title=\"West Country Water and Environment\"\u003eWCWE\u003c/abbr\u003e geography, with industry the biggest non-\u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e user in the region at 62%, followed by agriculture at 26%. In \u003cabbr title=\"Water Resources East\"\u003eWRE\u003c/abbr\u003e, agriculture is the largest non-\u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e water user at 43%, followed by the power generation sector at 31%. For the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Resource North\"\u003eWReN\u003c/abbr\u003e region, the largest non-\u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e user is the power generation sector at 54%, followed by industry at 26%, and agriculture at 18%. In the \u003cabbr title=\"Water Resources South East\"\u003eWRSE\u003c/abbr\u003e region, agriculture use at 35% is the largest water user outside of \u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e, closely followed by industry at 28%.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Water Resources East\"\u003eWRE\u003c/abbr\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Water Resources West\"\u003eWRW\u003c/abbr\u003e have the highest current consumptive water abstraction across the regional groups with 370 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e and 334 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e respectively.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"forecast-demands\"\u003e3.3.2 Forecast demands\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe analysis in 3.3.1 is based on how water is currently used outside the water industry. This section explores how water use in other sectors may change in the future. This is based on work undertaken for the first National Framework (2020) by Defra and a team of sector experts. This work examined the drivers for, and uncertainties in, water demand outside of public-water supply and provided best and upper estimate growth factors for the following sectors:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003espray irrigation\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003elivestock\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eprotected edible crops\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003efood and drink manufacturing\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eelectricity production\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003epaper and pulp\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003echemicals manufacturing\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThese sectors were selected as they cover a significant proportion of current water use (in total, more than 60% of consumptive freshwater direct abstraction arising from outside of the water industry).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePlease refer to \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/meeting-our-future-water-needs-a-national-framework-for-water-resources\"\u003eAppendix 5 of the 2020 National Framework\u003c/a\u003e for the detailed approach and results.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo forecast future non-\u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e demands, a combination of estimated growth factors used in the first National Framework and refined growth factors for specific sectors and regional groups were applied to a baseline (actual average abstraction from 2016 to 2021). These provide a ‘best estimate’ and an ‘upper’ estimate to explore sensitivities. A limitation of this approach is that it does not represent new abstraction emerging in locations where it does not take place already.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"figure-14-potential-changes-in-water-consumption-up-to-the-2050s-for-different-sectors-across-non-pws\"\u003eFigure 14: Potential changes in water consumption up to the 2050s for different \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e11.88\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e36.43\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e132.34\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e8.36\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e20.80\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e429.04\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003cp\u003eFigure 14 shows 3 scenarios. ‘Baseline’ represents average abstraction from 2016 to 2021, accounted for consumption. ‘Best estimate’ represents our assessment of the most likely estimate based on the evidence available. ‘Upper’ illustrates a reasonable upper estimate of possible water consumption. It shows an increase in demand for water not supplied by water companies for all sectors. For the sectors we have not looked at in detail there is no ‘best’ or ‘upper’ estimate and are taken as current baseline.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOf the sectors we have explored in detail, nationally, spray irrigation has a high projected increase in water consumption from a baseline consumptive recent actual abstraction of 240 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e to a reasonable upper estimate of 410 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e in the 2050s; a potential increase of 170 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e. This is closely followed by the power generation (electricity production) sector, demonstrating a potential upper estimate increase of 190 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e of water consumption by the 2050s to 470 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e from a baseline position of 280 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e. Nationally, the food and drink, chemicals and paper and pulp sectors show a potential upper estimate increase of 30, 20 and 5 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e of water consumption respectively; increasing to 90, 60 and 24 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e respectively by the 2050s. In total across all sectors, nationally, this equates to an additional non-public water need of around 400 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e (adjusted for consumptiveness) by the 2050s.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis analysis does not include other industry sectors, which currently account for the highest proportion of non-\u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e use (37%) at 320 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e recent actual water consumption. If these demands were to increase by 6% (based on national average projections of non-household water use supplied by water companies in their \u003cabbr title=\"water resources management plans\"\u003eWRMPs\u003c/abbr\u003e), this would equate to 24 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e of additional non-public water demands.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegional water resources groups, where spray irrigation and power generation sectors are dominant, display the highest projected increase in water consumption by the 2050s as shown in Figure 14. This includes \u003cabbr title=\"Water Resources East\"\u003eWRE\u003c/abbr\u003e (spray irrigation and power generation), \u003cabbr title=\"Water Resources West\"\u003eWRW\u003c/abbr\u003e (spray irrigation and power generation) and \u003cabbr title=\"Water Resource North\"\u003eWReN\u003c/abbr\u003e (power generation).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn all the sectors examined in detail, the potential increase in demand remains lower than the total volume currently licensed for abstraction nationally. However, abstractors should not assume they can always meet future growth by using volumes of water held on their existing licences that has been historically unused. It may be that in some catchments, an increased amount of abstraction could lead to further deterioration of environmental issues.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt is important that all sectors assess and plan for their future needs and understand how pressures on the water environment such as a changing climate may affect the future availability of water they rely on now.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"figure-15-potential-future-changes-upper-estimate-in-water-consumption-for-different-sectors-across-non-pws-comparing-to-potential-future-water-available-under-licences-once-environmental-requirements-are-considered-environmental-requirements-shown-are-the-fully-licenced-fl-abstractions-under-the-full-environmental-destination-planning-scenario-under-a-drier-range-in-the-2050s\"\u003eFigure 15: Potential future changes (upper estimate) in water consumption for different sectors across non-\u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e comparing to potential future water available under licences once environmental requirements are considered. Environmental requirements shown are the fully licenced (\u003cabbr title=\"fully licenced\"\u003eFL\u003c/abbr\u003e) abstractions, under the full Environmental Destination planning scenario under a drier range in the 2050s.\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e22.50\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e22.41\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e46.70\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e211.04\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e11.26\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e43.62\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e637.10\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003cp\u003eFigure 15 considers the upper estimate of potential future water consumption across non-\u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e and compares this to the amount of water existing licence holders can use once environmental requirements have been considered under the Full Environmental Destination planning scenario (under a drier range climate scenario in the 2050s). At a high level, all regional groups except for \u003cabbr title=\"West Country Water and Environment\"\u003eWCWE\u003c/abbr\u003e have enough water within the total volume of future licences, once environmental needs are considered, to accommodate future growth as estimated here. For some regions (\u003cabbr title=\"Water Resources South East\"\u003eWRSE\u003c/abbr\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Water Resource North\"\u003eWReN\u003c/abbr\u003e), this comparison is very close, with less than 6 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e spare in total volume of licences when compared to the upper estimate of demand increases. For \u003cabbr title=\"West Country Water and Environment\"\u003eWCWE\u003c/abbr\u003e upper estimates of future growth exceed the total volume of future licences when environmental requirements are accounted for. This varies significantly on a sector and licence basis, where for every sector in almost every region, a select number of abstractions would be limited by their annual licensed limit once environmental needs are accounted for, under the upper range of demand increases.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis comparison of future estimates of non-public water needs and potential future licensed volumes, taking account of potential climate impacts and environmental requirements, highlights the importance of promoting water rights trading amongst non-\u003cabbr title=\"public water supply\"\u003ePWS\u003c/abbr\u003e users. Water rights trading within and across sectors, as well as within regions (and even across regions in some geographies), has the potential to help ensure water is available when it is needed for non-public water users in the future.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe will continue to work with regional groups and water using sectors to help them prioritise work to better forecast water needs. This is particularly relevant where there are emerging new demands that are not reflected in this analysis; those sectors need to work with regional groups as far as possible to try and plan for this. As an example, the work undertaken and described in detail in Section 7 on future energy needs, predict a national additional consumptive need of 767 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e by the 2050s for hydrogen and carbon capture storage (\u003cabbr title=\"carbon capture and storage\"\u003eCCS\u003c/abbr\u003e) alone. When combined with our future estimates of non-public water needs, the total additional consumptive water requirements for other sectors by the 2050s are estimated to be 1,090 \u003cabbr title=\"megalitres per day\"\u003eMl/d\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"call-to-action\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003eNext: \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-framework-for-water-resources-2025-water-for-growth-nature-and-a-resilient-future/4-water-availability-national-framework-for-water-resources-2025\"\u003e4. Water availability\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e"
      }
    }
  ]

  <h1 class="gem-c-heading__text govuk-heading-xl">
    3. How much additional water we need: National Framework for Water Resources 2025
</h1></div>

    <p class="gem-c-inverse-header__subtext">Updated 27 August 2026</p>
</header>



  
  <section data-ga4-devolved-nations-banner="England, Wales" data-module="ga4-link-tracker" data-ga4-set-indexes="" data-ga4-link='{"event_name":"navigation","type":"devolved nations banner","section":"Applies to England and Wales"}' aria-label="Nation" class="gem-c-devolved-nations">
    <h2 class="govuk-heading-s govuk-!-margin-bottom-0">
      Applies to England and Wales
</h2>
</section>

  <div data-module="govspeak" class="gem-c-govspeak gem-c-govspeak--direction-ltr govuk-!-margin-bottom-0">
    
    
        <div class="govspeak"><p>The modelling of scenarios of population growth, climate change and environmental sustainability reductions demonstrates that without action, there could be a public water supply (<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr>) deficit of up to 5,000 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> by 2055. Additional pressure will result from other sectors of use, particularly from the energy, food and data centre sectors. Non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> sectors alone will account for an additional demand of 1,200 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> by the 2050s.</p>

<p>The National Framework provides a picture of water needs across the country by 2055. Figure 4 shows the forecast water needs for each regional group in England. The estimated additional public water needs are based on the Do Nothing modelled scenario. The Do Nothing scenario assumptions are explained in section 2.2. The forecasts for future non-public water needs are presented as the estimated total demand for 2055, including current demands and are based on an upper estimate scenario that considers recent actual abstraction adjusted for consumptiveness, with relevant sector-based growth factors applied. The forecasts exclude coastal, tidal and estuarine abstractions as well as abstraction related to navigation. The forecasts do not include new or emerging non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> demands such as low carbon energy or data centres. The non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> forecast approach is explained in further detail in section 3.2.</p>

<h3 id="figure-4-understanding-englands-future-water-needs-by-2055">Figure 4: Understanding England’s future water needs by 2055</h3>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/681cb4cb3f1c73824ee3e5df/s960_Figure-4-understanding-England_s-future-water-needs-by-20255.png" alt=""></div></figure>

<p>For <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr>, the estimated <strong>additional</strong> water need between 2030 and 2055 includes the key drivers:</p>

<ul>
  <li>increasing resilience to a 1 in 500-year drought</li>
  <li>high population growth</li>
  <li>high environmental improvement through delivery of the most ambitious reductions identified in current water company plans</li>
  <li>individual water company analysis of climate change impacts</li>
</ul>

<p>There are also other factors influencing the water supply by 2055, not captured above, which will result in both increases and decreases in total water availability across each region.</p>

<p>We also show the <strong>upper</strong> estimate forecast of the proportion of consumptive water used by the different sectors in each region. We have shortened million litres per day to <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>.</p>

<h3 id="water-resources-west-wrw">Water Resources West (<abbr title="Water Resources West">WRW</abbr>)</h3>

<p>The map shows the full area of <abbr title="Water Resources West">WRW</abbr> including parts of Wales. The values also include Welsh zones within the boundary, but the headline figures in the Framework do not.</p>

<p>Additional <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> needs between 2030 and 2055 are <strong>1,073 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr></strong> including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>drought resilience: 62 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>population change: 232 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>environmental improvement: 572 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>climate change: 84 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
</ul>

<p>Estimated total demand from other users is <strong>429 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr></strong>:</p>

<ul>
  <li>49% industry (food and drink, metal production, chemicals)</li>
  <li>27% agriculture (spray irrigation)</li>
  <li>17% power generation</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="water-resources-north-wren">Water Resources North (<abbr title="Water Resource North">WReN</abbr>)</h3>

<p>Additional <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> needs between 2030 and 2055 are <strong>345 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr></strong> including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>drought resilience: 70 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>population change: 99 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>environmental improvement: 109 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>climate change: 60 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
</ul>

<p>Estimated total demand from other users is <strong>261 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr></strong>:</p>

<ul>
  <li>22% industry (food and drink, chemicals, mineral products)</li>
  <li>17% agriculture (spray irrigation)</li>
  <li>59% power generation</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="water-resources-east-wre">Water Resources East (<abbr title="Water Resources East">WRE</abbr>)</h3>

<p>Additional <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> needs between 2030 and 2055 are <strong>679 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr></strong> including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>drought resilience: 114 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>population change: 165 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>environmental improvement: 415 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>climate change: 26 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
</ul>

<p>Estimated total demand from other users is <strong>564 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr></strong>:</p>

<ul>
  <li>11% industry (food and drink, chemicals, mineral products)</li>
  <li>47% agriculture (spray irrigation)</li>
  <li>34% power generation</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="west-country-water-and-environment-wcwe">West Country Water and Environment (<abbr title="West Country Water and Environment">WCWE</abbr>)</h3>

<p>Additional <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> needs between 2030 and 2055 are <strong>260 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr></strong> including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>drought resilience: 5 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>population change: 85 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>environmental improvement: 182 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>climate change: 20 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
</ul>

<p>Estimated total demand from other users is <strong>216 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr></strong>:</p>

<ul>
  <li>60% industry (food and drink, chemicals, mineral products)</li>
  <li>26% agriculture (spray irrigation)</li>
  <li>1% power generation</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="water-resources-south-east-wrse">Water Resources South East (<abbr title="Water Resources South East">WRSE</abbr>)</h3>

<p>Additional <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> needs between 2030 and 2055 are <strong>2,034 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr></strong> including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>drought resilience: 377 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>population change: 424 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>environmental improvement: 1,350 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>climate change: 161 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
</ul>

<p>Estimated total demand from other users is <strong>150 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr></strong>:</p>

<ul>
  <li>23% industry (food and drink, chemicals, mineral products)</li>
  <li>35% agriculture (spray irrigation)</li>
  <li>31% power generation</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="environmental-needs">3.1 Environmental needs</h2>

<p>The quantification of changes to current and future abstraction needed to meet environmental requirements is known as the Environmental Destination for water resources.</p>

<div role="note" aria-label="Information" class="application-notice info-notice">
  <p>The <strong>Environmental Destination</strong> for water resources identifies where, and by how much, water abstraction needs to change to achieve and maintain a healthy water environment, both now and in the future.</p>
</div>

<p>The Environmental Destination defines the long-term environmental outcomes to ensure abstraction from rivers, groundwater, lakes, wetlands and estuaries is environmentally sustainable, both to address current unsustainable abstraction and future pressures. ​​It identifies where and by how much abstraction may need to reduce to meet current and future environmental requirements for nature. It considers both legal requirements and government commitments. It includes known challenges and assessments of the future potential impact of climate change and considers growth.</p>

<p>The detailed technical approach to assessing environmental needs is contained in Appendix C: Environmental Destination technical report. This includes how we use this includes how we use environmental flow targets to identify where changes to abstraction may be required.</p>

<p>The figures presented here are a high-level indication of need. They have been adjusted downwards to reflect the actions already included in the 2024 round of water company water resources management plans. They are based on national data sets and analysis and do not include where there may be additional local environmental requirements. They have not been adjusted to reflect any ‘overriding public interest’ decisions which may be made in the future. The figures may also need to be refined as the growth agenda is reflected in Regional Water Resources Plans.</p>

<p>They allow for better evidence to be used to refine the assessments locally and are the starting point for regional water resources groups to take the national figures and to refine them as they develop regional plans. We will provide supplementary technical guidance to advise regional groups on how to include Environmental Destination needs within their plans. Where water companies have sources within or affecting Wales (to supply England), Natural Resources Wales provides guidance on how to meet Welsh legislation Environmental Destination requirements.</p>

<h3 id="figure-5-environmental-requirements-at-a-water-body-level">Figure 5: Environmental requirements at a water body level</h3>

<p>These maps show river waterbodies where abstraction may need to be reduced to meet environment needs at a Q95 low flow. Three maps show the potential abstraction reduction that may be needed now and by the 2050s.</p>

<h4 id="map-1-current-situation-potential-abstraction-reduction-by-waterbody-in-todays-climate">Map 1: Current situation: potential abstraction reduction by waterbody in today’s climate</h4>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/684069b31d85c6606009cd54/s960_Figure-5-Map-1.png" alt=""></div></figure>

<p>Map 1 shows potential abstraction reductions against today’s baseline environmental requirements. The baseline shows that there is a potential need to reduce fully licensed abstraction by up to 3,200 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> to address current unsustainable abstraction. Of the total estimated abstraction reductions required to meet environmental requirements, approximately 60% is to address current unsustainable abstraction, and of this, water company abstraction accounts for approximately 90% of the reductions needed.</p>

<h4 id="map-2-situation-with-climate-change-and-full-environmental-expectations-potential-abstraction-reduction-by-waterbody-in-2050">Map 2: Situation with climate change and full environmental expectations: potential abstraction reduction by waterbody in 2050</h4>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/684069bbe550203c8209cd45/s960_Figure-5-Map-2.png" alt=""></div></figure>

<p>Map 2 shows how this may change by the 2050s with inclusion of full environmental expectations and with climate change (dry scenario). For this scenario, by the 2050s, this total need could rise to 5,400 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> (full expectations).</p>

<h4 id="map-3-situation-with-climate-change-full-environmental-expectations-and-after-wrmp24-actions-delivered-potential-abstraction-reduction-by-waterbody-in-2050">Map 3: Situation with climate change, full environmental expectations and after <abbr title="water resource management plan 24">WRMP24</abbr> actions delivered: potential abstraction reduction by waterbody in 2050</h4>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/684069c2cb73e8b12647b424/s960_Figure-5-Map-3.png" alt=""></div></figure>

<p>Map 3 shows the remaining potential abstraction reductions following delivery <abbr title="water resource management plan 24">WRMP24</abbr> actions (dry scenario). If we take account of plans identified in the 2024 round of water company water resources management plans the environmental requirements could reduce to 2,700 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> (full expectations).</p>

<p>The <a rel="external" href="https://engageenvironmentagency.uk.engagementhq.com/data-publications-water">data behind these maps is available from the Environment Agency’s Water Hub</a> and is presented at a water body scale.</p>

<p>For an explanation of the development and history of the Environmental Destination figures, please see our technical report. This explains how the figures have evolved and how our understanding of the scale of the challenge has improved.</p>

<p>The Environmental Destination will result in a pressure on some, but not all, abstraction licences in those water bodies identified in the analysis. For public water supplies, this is likely to drive a need for additional options to ensure that water remains in the environment.</p>

<p>Environmental Destination quantifies the potential reductions that could potentially be required to abstraction to meet these environmental requirements. By presenting this analysis, it could be interpreted that there will be a need to require abstraction reductions across all licences in a catchment as the solution. This is not the case. Many abstractions will already be environmentally sustainable because they include conditions to protect flows and levels; for example, some licences will authorise abstraction to fill storage reservoirs at high flows only, avoiding pressures on low flows. The licences most at risk of change will be permanent licences in areas of greatest water stress which do not adequately protect protected site objectives, low flows or groundwater levels.</p>

<p>Addressing unsustainable abstractions will affect supply/demand balances across all sectors of use and will drive the need for additional demand management activity and resource development (in sustainable sources). We set out our approach for action in Section 5.</p>

<p>We will continue to refine our assessment of environmental need. In determining future environmental requirements, we will recognise that as climate change impacts are felt by the environment, natural flows will change, and the environmental needs of the future will reflect this changed environment. We will look at how abstraction licensing should accommodate these changing needs and how protection should be provided for important water dependent nature conservation sites within this evolving landscape, whilst providing a framework for water users to effectively plan water resources for the future.</p>

<h2 id="pws-needs">3.2 <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> needs</h2>

<p>By 2055, the nation will need up to an additional 5 billion litres of water per day for <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> under a Do Nothing scenario. This is enough to fill Wembley Stadium almost 4.5 times every day.</p>

<p>The previous National Framework for Water Resources (2020) identified that up to 3,435 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> would be needed from <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> between 2020 and 2050 without continued action.</p>

<p>This was revised upwards to 4,800 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> by 2050 in 2024 following water company assessments in water resources management plans. The increase was due to updated demand forecasts, additional reductions associated with protecting and improving the environment, and better representation of the baseline supply position without drought measures included.</p>

<p>The modelling for the 2025 National Framework for Water Resources shows that the headline deficit is 4,940 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> by 2055.</p>

<div role="note" aria-label="Information" class="application-notice info-notice">
  <p>Our modelling work uses a baseline of 2030 and takes account of the ambitious delivery of actions outlined from 2025 to 2030 in water company water resource management plans. If delivered fully, these actions reduce the deficit to 4,370 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> by 2055. This figure is used in our detailed modelling analysis.</p>
</div>

<p>Nationally, as highlighted in Figure 6, <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> accounts for 87% of current water consumption based on fully licensed abstractions. Of <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr>, water use from households (<abbr title="household">HH</abbr>) currently accounts for 58% of water put into supply. This is followed by non-households (<abbr title="non-households">NHH</abbr>), such as businesses and industry with use at around 20%. Leakage still makes up a large percentage of current <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> use, at 19%.</p>

<p>Current <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> availability is already under pressure. Figure 7 highlights that in 2025, there are already water resource zones without a surplus. Nationally, the average availability in 2025 across water resource zones is approximately 7 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>. In some parts of England, water companies are not currently accepting requests for new water for some new non-domestic supplies. This could affect economic growth.</p>

<p>Figure 8 shows the range of national future <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> needs by 2055 under the modelled scenarios (referred to as supply demand balance). This could range from 0 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> (where we see a surplus of almost 2,320 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> under the Low water needs scenario) to an additional need (deficit) of up to 4,370 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> under the Do Nothing scenario. This is a range of around 6,700 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>. Even with the delivery of all the resource development in company plans and 60% of the demand management reductions currently planned (as presented in the High water needs scenario) there is still a deficit. It shows that delivery of the actions identified through water resources planning (under Central and Low scenarios) can achieve a surplus but strongly highlights the importance of delivering resource development and demand management actions in current plans to resolve those deficits.</p>

<p>The national pressures that contribute to the overall supply-demand-balance vary significantly across each of the modelled scenarios as highlighted in Figure 9.</p>

<p>Future water needs will vary at a regional, water company and water resource zone scales across the modelled scenarios. This is outlined in Figure 9. Whilst the nation may observe an overall surplus, there are still deficits observed at a water company resource zone scale. The full range of modelled outputs are described in detail at the regional scale in Appendix A.</p>

<h3 id="figure-9-future-pws-availability-under-the-modelled-scenarios-maps">Figure 9: Future <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> availability under the modelled scenarios (maps)</h3>

<p>Key:</p>

<ul>
  <li>darkest red: -700 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
  <li>darkest blue: 700 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>
</li>
</ul>

<p>Under two of the modelled scenarios, England will observe a water supply deficit in 2055. The reduction in supply to meet environmental needs accounts for over half of the total deficit under both scenarios (around 57% under the Do Nothing scenario).</p>

<h3 id="figure-10-the-drivers-of-the-national-deficit-by-2055-under-the-do-nothing-scenario-mld">Figure 10: The drivers of the national deficit by 2055 under the Do Nothing scenario (<abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>)</h3>

<table class="js-barchart-table mc-auto-outdent">
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Driver</th>
      <th scope="col"><abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr></th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Demand from household growth</th>
      <td>990</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Resilience move to 0.2% annual chance of drought failure</th>
      <td>630</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Climate change impact to supply</th>
      <td>340</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Environmental needs impact on supply</th>
      <td>2,600</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p>As shown in Figure 10, under the Do Nothing scenario, the water required to meet the needs of the environment is the biggest driver of future need at a national level, with 2,600 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> forecast to be required by 2055 due to reductions in abstraction to meet current legal environmental requirements and government ambition (taken from <abbr title="water resource management plan 24">WRMP24</abbr>). Nationally, demand from household population growth is the second biggest driver of the deficit under Do Nothing with an increase of 990 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> of additional need compared to current baseline. A major component of the last round of <abbr title="water resources management plans">WRMPs</abbr> was to ensure that there is increased water supply resilience for people and business where systems are expected to be resilient to a 0.2% annual chance of failure caused by a drought (meaning a 1:500 return period) by 2039. This increased resilience adds an additional 630 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> to the Do Nothing deficit by 2055 under all scenarios at a national scale compared to the baseline. The changing climate puts additional pressure on water availability. Climate change as a driver for future demand is forecast to impact supply by 340 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>. Please note that Figure 10 only shows the main drivers and does not represent all components of the supply demand balance. For more information, please refer to the water resources modelling technical report.</p>

<p>The individual and combined pressures on public water supplies can also be shown at a water company water resource zone scale. Figure 11 shows how climate change, environmental needs, population, drought resilience and in combination pressures drive a need for additional capacity between 2030 and 2055. The figure quantifies this pressure as <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> as a proportion of water supplied (distribution input) in each water company water resources zone, under the Do Nothing scenario.</p>

<h3 id="figure-11-the-total-estimated-additional-capacity-required-to-meet-each-pressure-individually-and-in-combination-by-2055-as-a-proportion-of-the-water-supplied-distribution-input-under-a-do-nothing-scenario">Figure 11: The total estimated additional capacity required to meet each pressure individually and in combination by 2055 (as a proportion of the water supplied (distribution input)) under a Do Nothing scenario</h3>

<p>Key for <abbr title="distribution input">DI</abbr>:</p>

<ul>
  <li>darkest red: -200% of <abbr title="distribution input">DI</abbr> at 2030</li>
  <li>darkest blue: 200% of <abbr title="distribution input">DI</abbr> at 2030</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="direct-abstraction-the-needs-of-other-sectors">3.3 Direct abstraction: the needs of other sectors</h2>

<p>Our future estimates of non-public water needs, show that the total additional consumptive water requirements for other sectors by the 2050s could be 1090 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>. This includes an assessment of future water needs for carbon capture and storage and hydrogen production which estimates that 767 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> will be needed by 2050 (see chapter 7).</p>

<p>Nationally, spray irrigation has a high projected increase in water consumption with a potential increase of 170 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>. The food and drink, chemicals and paper and pulp sectors show a potential increase of 30, 20 and 5 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> of water consumption respectively by the 2050s.</p>

<h3 id="baseline-use">3.3.1 Baseline use</h3>

<p>It is not just water companies that provide water for business and water using sectors. Water users who abstract directly from the water environment are currently licensed for 114,000 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> and abstract 28,000 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> of freshwater from rivers and groundwater. This demand is forecast to increase to 33,000 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> by the 2050s (not adjusted for consumptiveness).</p>

<p>Figure 12 shows current estimated proportion of abstraction from freshwater by purpose and adjusted for consumptiveness, excluding navigation. The charts show both excluding and including <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> . <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> is the largest water abstractor.</p>

<p>(Abstraction related to navigation has been excluded from this assessment. This is because not all abstractions and transfers to support navigation have been represented in the <abbr title="water resources geographical information systems">WRGIS</abbr> abstraction datasets used in this assessment; some navigation transfers may have been accounted for elsewhere as complex activities in the <abbr title="water resources geographical information systems">WRGIS</abbr>. For more information on abstracted related to navigation, please refer to the water resources modelling technical report.)</p>

<p>If <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> use is excluded, under recent actual abstraction rates (and adjusted for consumptiveness), the industry sector uses the most water nationally at 37%, followed by agriculture (30%) and then power (23%). Under fully licensed quantities (adjusted for consumptiveness) the split is very similar to recent actual, with the industry sector at 34%, agriculture at 33% and power generation reduced to 20%.</p>

<p>Figure 13 shows the current recent actual consumptive water abstraction from freshwater outside the water industry, excluding navigation. The graphs show how this differs across the regional groups. In the <abbr title="Water Resources West">WRW</abbr> geography, industry is the biggest non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> water user at 56%, followed by agriculture at 23%. This is a similar pattern in the <abbr title="West Country Water and Environment">WCWE</abbr> geography, with industry the biggest non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> user in the region at 62%, followed by agriculture at 26%. In <abbr title="Water Resources East">WRE</abbr>, agriculture is the largest non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> water user at 43%, followed by the power generation sector at 31%. For the <abbr title="Water Resource North">WReN</abbr> region, the largest non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> user is the power generation sector at 54%, followed by industry at 26%, and agriculture at 18%. In the <abbr title="Water Resources South East">WRSE</abbr> region, agriculture use at 35% is the largest water user outside of <abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr>, closely followed by industry at 28%.</p>

<p><abbr title="Water Resources East">WRE</abbr> and <abbr title="Water Resources West">WRW</abbr> have the highest current consumptive water abstraction across the regional groups with 370 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> and 334 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> respectively.</p>

<h3 id="forecast-demands">3.3.2 Forecast demands</h3>

<p>The analysis in 3.3.1 is based on how water is currently used outside the water industry. This section explores how water use in other sectors may change in the future. This is based on work undertaken for the first National Framework (2020) by Defra and a team of sector experts. This work examined the drivers for, and uncertainties in, water demand outside of public-water supply and provided best and upper estimate growth factors for the following sectors:</p>

<ul>
  <li>spray irrigation</li>
  <li>livestock</li>
  <li>protected edible crops</li>
  <li>food and drink manufacturing</li>
  <li>electricity production</li>
  <li>paper and pulp</li>
  <li>chemicals manufacturing</li>
</ul>

<p>These sectors were selected as they cover a significant proportion of current water use (in total, more than 60% of consumptive freshwater direct abstraction arising from outside of the water industry).</p>

<p>Please refer to <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/meeting-our-future-water-needs-a-national-framework-for-water-resources">Appendix 5 of the 2020 National Framework</a> for the detailed approach and results.</p>

<p>To forecast future non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> demands, a combination of estimated growth factors used in the first National Framework and refined growth factors for specific sectors and regional groups were applied to a baseline (actual average abstraction from 2016 to 2021). These provide a ‘best estimate’ and an ‘upper’ estimate to explore sensitivities. A limitation of this approach is that it does not represent new abstraction emerging in locations where it does not take place already.</p>

<h3 id="figure-14-potential-changes-in-water-consumption-up-to-the-2050s-for-different-sectors-across-non-pws">Figure 14: Potential changes in water consumption up to the 2050s for different sectors across non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr>

      <th scope="col" class="cell-text-right">Other agriculture</th>
      <th scope="col" class="cell-text-right">Chemicals</th>
      <th scope="col" class="cell-text-right">Paper and pulp</th>
      <th scope="col" class="cell-text-right">Food and drink</th>
      <th scope="col">Other industry</th>
      <th scope="col">Private water supply</th>
      <th scope="col">Other non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> sectors</th>
      <th scope="col">Total</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Baseline</th>
      <td class="cell-text-right">54.00</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">43.15</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">19.81</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">22.46</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">9.52</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">23.64</td>
      <td>132.32</td>
      <td>8.36</td>
      <td>20.80</td>
      <td>334.06</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Best estimate</th>
      <td class="cell-text-right">77.77</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">52.64</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">24.17</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">22.68</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">10.67</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">29.54</td>
      <td>132.33</td>
      <td>8.36</td>
      <td>20.80</td>
      <td>378.95</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Upper estimate</th>
      <td class="cell-text-right">93.83</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">71.63</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">31.09</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">22.68</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">11.88</td>
      <td class="cell-text-right">36.43</td>
      <td>132.34</td>
      <td>8.36</td>
      <td>20.80</td>
      <td>429.04</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p>Figure 14 shows 3 scenarios. ‘Baseline’ represents average abstraction from 2016 to 2021, accounted for consumption. ‘Best estimate’ represents our assessment of the most likely estimate based on the evidence available. ‘Upper’ illustrates a reasonable upper estimate of possible water consumption. It shows an increase in demand for water not supplied by water companies for all sectors. For the sectors we have not looked at in detail there is no ‘best’ or ‘upper’ estimate and are taken as current baseline.</p>

<p>Of the sectors we have explored in detail, nationally, spray irrigation has a high projected increase in water consumption from a baseline consumptive recent actual abstraction of 240 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> to a reasonable upper estimate of 410 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> in the 2050s; a potential increase of 170 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>. This is closely followed by the power generation (electricity production) sector, demonstrating a potential upper estimate increase of 190 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> of water consumption by the 2050s to 470 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> from a baseline position of 280 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>. Nationally, the food and drink, chemicals and paper and pulp sectors show a potential upper estimate increase of 30, 20 and 5 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> of water consumption respectively; increasing to 90, 60 and 24 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> respectively by the 2050s. In total across all sectors, nationally, this equates to an additional non-public water need of around 400 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> (adjusted for consumptiveness) by the 2050s.</p>

<p>This analysis does not include other industry sectors, which currently account for the highest proportion of non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> use (37%) at 320 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> recent actual water consumption. If these demands were to increase by 6% (based on national average projections of non-household water use supplied by water companies in their <abbr title="water resources management plans">WRMPs</abbr>), this would equate to 24 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> of additional non-public water demands.</p>

<p>Regional water resources groups, where spray irrigation and power generation sectors are dominant, display the highest projected increase in water consumption by the 2050s as shown in Figure 14. This includes <abbr title="Water Resources East">WRE</abbr> (spray irrigation and power generation), <abbr title="Water Resources West">WRW</abbr> (spray irrigation and power generation) and <abbr title="Water Resource North">WReN</abbr> (power generation).</p>

<p>In all the sectors examined in detail, the potential increase in demand remains lower than the total volume currently licensed for abstraction nationally. However, abstractors should not assume they can always meet future growth by using volumes of water held on their existing licences that has been historically unused. It may be that in some catchments, an increased amount of abstraction could lead to further deterioration of environmental issues.</p>

<p>It is important that all sectors assess and plan for their future needs and understand how pressures on the water environment such as a changing climate may affect the future availability of water they rely on now.</p>

<h3 id="figure-15-potential-future-changes-upper-estimate-in-water-consumption-for-different-sectors-across-non-pws-comparing-to-potential-future-water-available-under-licences-once-environmental-requirements-are-considered-environmental-requirements-shown-are-the-fully-licenced-fl-abstractions-under-the-full-environmental-destination-planning-scenario-under-a-drier-range-in-the-2050s">Figure 15: Potential future changes (upper estimate) in water consumption for different sectors across non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> comparing to potential future water available under licences once environmental requirements are considered. Environmental requirements shown are the fully licenced (<abbr title="fully licenced">FL</abbr>) abstractions, under the full Environmental Destination planning scenario under a drier range in the 2050s.</h3>

<p>Figure 15 considers the upper estimate of potential future water consumption across non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> and compares this to the amount of water existing licence holders can use once environmental requirements have been considered under the Full Environmental Destination planning scenario (under a drier range climate scenario in the 2050s). At a high level, all regional groups except for <abbr title="West Country Water and Environment">WCWE</abbr> have enough water within the total volume of future licences, once environmental needs are considered, to accommodate future growth as estimated here. For some regions (<abbr title="Water Resources South East">WRSE</abbr> and <abbr title="Water Resource North">WReN</abbr>), this comparison is very close, with less than 6 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> spare in total volume of licences when compared to the upper estimate of demand increases. For <abbr title="West Country Water and Environment">WCWE</abbr> upper estimates of future growth exceed the total volume of future licences when environmental requirements are accounted for. This varies significantly on a sector and licence basis, where for every sector in almost every region, a select number of abstractions would be limited by their annual licensed limit once environmental needs are accounted for, under the upper range of demand increases.</p>

<p>This comparison of future estimates of non-public water needs and potential future licensed volumes, taking account of potential climate impacts and environmental requirements, highlights the importance of promoting water rights trading amongst non-<abbr title="public water supply">PWS</abbr> users. Water rights trading within and across sectors, as well as within regions (and even across regions in some geographies), has the potential to help ensure water is available when it is needed for non-public water users in the future.</p>

<p>We will continue to work with regional groups and water using sectors to help them prioritise work to better forecast water needs. This is particularly relevant where there are emerging new demands that are not reflected in this analysis; those sectors need to work with regional groups as far as possible to try and plan for this. As an example, the work undertaken and described in detail in Section 7 on future energy needs, predict a national additional consumptive need of 767 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr> by the 2050s for hydrogen and carbon capture storage (<abbr title="carbon capture and storage">CCS</abbr>) alone. When combined with our future estimates of non-public water needs, the total additional consumptive water requirements for other sectors by the 2050s are estimated to be 1,090 <abbr title="megalitres per day">Ml/d</abbr>.</p>

</div>
